note: A retirement is a preservation claim, not a story about a red run. Every entry registers the retired path (file), the original path it was retired from (original_path), the sha256 of the preserved bytes (the retirement's retired_sha256), the commit those bytes are claimed to come from (retired_from_commit), a free-text reason, the registration date (retired_on) and the review that accepted the retirement (review_reference). scripts/verify-retirement-registry.js reads no test output. It checks five things from files, hashes and the object store: (a) preserved - the file at the registered path hashes to the registered sha256; (b) complete - every file under tests/legacy/ is registered; (c) not a fake retirement - the original path does not still carry the registered bytes; (d) re-evaluable - the registered bytes are put back at the original path and run, and a passing run is named as a receipt (KDNA-RETIREMENT-RESTORABLE) because the entry is not stale; (e) zero rewrite - the registered sha256 is the sha256 of the bytes at original_path in retired_from_commit, read from the object store, so the copy under tests/legacy/ is byte for byte the file that was at the original path. Only (a)-(c) and (e) decide the exit code. Each retired copy here is the pre-retirement file itself: the move into tests/legacy/ changed nothing, not even a relative require, because nothing under tests/legacy/ is ever run. The suites are red against the committed graph because the objects they exercise are gone from it; that is recorded as an independent observation in the delivery report, and a file that would only fit tests/legacy/ after being adapted is not retired at all.
